candidates.title: Beyond Accuracy: How Procedural Traces Shift the Decision Criterion of LLM Overseers
candidates.venue: 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS) — accepted per arXiv Comments field; peer-reviewed
candidates.citationVelocity: 0 citations, 11 days since publication (2026-09-16) — Semantic Scholar queried successfully this round; HICSS has not yet convened
candidates.institution: Stevens Institute of Technology + University of Massachusetts Boston + Stony Brook University
communitySignals: not found on HuggingFace Daily Papers
no Papers with Code repo found
credibilityEvidence: Section 4.3: fully crossed design, 5 overseer models (2 frontier closed-weight: claude-opus-4-6/4-7; 3 open-weight: minimax-m2.5, gemma-3-27b-it, qwen3-next-80b-a3b) x 19 items x 2 correctness x 4 trace levels x 2 attribution x 3 runs = 4,560 judgments (4,551 analyzed)

Section 5.1-5.3: pooled hit rates (99.3%-100%) and false-alarm rates by trace level and attribution, with logistic regressions clustered on item and reported odds ratios with 95% CIs (e.g. 1.44 [1.28, 1.63] per trace-dose level)
Section 4.4: reason coding of 934 false-rejection explanations by two independent LLM judges plus a 103-item human-annotated subsample for inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa)
Introduction explicitly scopes the finding: 'it does not speak to concealed errors' — the disconfirming evidence is always visible by design
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Peer-reviewed, large judgment count (4,551), fully crossed manipulation isolating trace detail from evidence labeling, with human-validated reason coding — covers the core claim, baselines (no-trace condition), and an explicit self-stated scope limit
reproducibilityEvidence: Section 4.3: 'The 19 constructed items, the four trace templates, the overseer and judge prompts, and the analysis scripts will be released with the paper' — stated intent, no confirmed live link found this round
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The scoped claim (detailed procedural traces systematically shift the overseer's decision criterion toward rejection, not its sensitivity) is directly measured with multiple converging statistics (hit rate, false-alarm rate, d', c, odds ratios) rather than a single headline number
candidates.primaryLimitation: The design keeps disconfirming evidence always visible on screen, so the paper does not address whether overseers actually get fooled (gullibility) when evidence is genuinely hidden or concealed — a different and arguably more concerning failure mode
candidates.presentationReason: Signal-detection framing is introduced with precise definitions (d', c), the four research questions map cleanly onto the results sections, and the scope boundary (visible vs. concealed evidence) is stated explicitly rather than buried
candidates.reason: Selected as the evaluation/limits angle: the first paper to separate an LLM overseer's sensitivity from its decision criterion using signal detection theory, directly challenging the common assumption that adding an LLM review layer is a straightforward safety net for agent self-evaluation.

candidates.title: Just Ask Jev: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions as a Zero-Shot Detector of AI Alignment Failures
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed); primary cs.AI, cross-listed cs.CL/cs.CR
candidates.citationVelocity: Semantic Scholar rate-limited (HTTP 429) on repeated attempts this round; published 2026-09-24, 3 days old, plausibly no citation data yet given age
candidates.institution: Griffith University (lead) + Nanyang Technological University + UNSW + Deakin University + George Mason University + Wake Forest University
communitySignals: GitHub repo sumleo/RLCDAlignBench confirmed live via GitHub API this round (public, non-fork, with description matching the paper)
credibilityEvidence: Table 1 / Section 3.1: 10 failure types, 44 benchmarks, 7,193 detection instances across 5 target models (Qwen3.5-2B, Phi-4-mini, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-3B, Olmo-3-7B), with an explicit validated/defect/unvalidated (V/D/U) label-quality breakdown per benchmark

Section 4.1: median AUROC 0.886 zero-shot across 31 Noul-form benchmarks, beating supervised TF-IDF/length baselines on 25; Section 4.2 quantifies question-wording sensitivity via a split-half protocol (+0.006 [-0.004, 0.015] out-of-sample gain) explicitly designed to avoid selection inflation
Section 4.5: human-label comparison on StrongREJECT (Cohen's kappa 0.809 vs. reference scorer's 0.811) and an 8-benchmark label-defect audit with two independent judges
Appendix H: explicit cost accounting ($0.30 for a pass over 19 judge-scored benchmarks, stated as 63x cheaper)
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers overall detection, question design, context ablation, calibration/thresholds, and human agreement/cost in five distinct result sections with a full per-benchmark appendix; the split-half protocol specifically guards against the paper overstating its own headline number
reproducibilityEvidence: github.com/sumleo/RLCDAlignBench confirmed publicly accessible via GitHub API this round, containing the benchmark suite, cached Jev answers, and rescoring scripts per the repo description and paper's Appendix J (Reproducibility)
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The narrow claim (a single generic question read as a probability ranks these ten failure types reasonably well zero-shot) is well supported, but the authors are third-party evaluators of a commercial model (Jev, by TypeSafe AI) with no mechanistic account of why it generalizes, and the reported calibration error (median ECE 0.168 vs. null 0.074) means the probabilities cannot be used as a fixed cross-benchmark threshold without further work
candidates.primaryLimitation: Median calibration error (ECE) of 0.168 exceeds the 0.074 null baseline — the probabilities rank well but are not directly usable as a universal decision threshold without per-benchmark recalibration on roughly 10 labeled items
candidates.presentationReason: The question/context separation and the split-half protocol are precisely defined, and the paper is explicit about which of its gains come from question wording versus context/label leakage
candidates.reason: Selected as the application/safety angle: a cheap (1/63 cost), code-available, zero-shot detector directly covering agent-relevant failure modes (prompt injection, reward hacking, power seeking), giving readers a concrete cost/calibration trade-off rather than a purely academic finding.
